Cass, can we stay up for the lanterns?
We can stay up forever.
Happy Kindling Eve, little bird.
Happy Kindling Eve, Mom.
And then it was morning.
Tomorrow never came. Nobody minded. Nobody ever would.
It was beautiful. It was the most beautiful day in the world.
It was the only one.
THE END?
The throne. The Shards hang in the air where the King came apart, turning slowly, like the hands of a clock.
On the steps, a man in scorched white robes kneels where the King fell. Smaller than you remember. Grayer.
_(barely a whisper)_ You said no.
To her. To her face. How could you— I couldn't. I never could. Not once in forty years.
I know. That's why you built all this.
Overhead, the hanging Shards begin to tick.
No. No — wait — I'm not singing it. I've stopped. I've stopped! I'm not—
It does not need you anymore. Listen.
Tick. Tick. Tick. Every clock in Evernoon, all at once. The Vespersong has been sung so long it has learned to sing itself.
The Shards lock together into a face. A clock with a sun for a dial and no numbers at all. Only noon, and noon, and noon.
Vesper
STAY.
Oh, I REALLY don't like that.
Cassian. What is that.
Then we're done going back.
Everyone — with me. One more time.
Something warm moves in Wren's chest — her mother's light, her own now — and runs through all six of them like a struck chord.
Vesper stops.
Not the way Evernoon stopped. The way a clock stops when it is finally, finally allowed to rest.
The seven Shards drift down into the middle of the throne room. Warm. Dim. Waiting.
Now. Put it back — put the sun back together!
The Shards rise. They turn. They try to fit, edge to edge, the way they were.
They don't fit.
Wren... it doesn't go. The edges have changed. They've been out in the world too long.
It remembers being a sun. Remembering is not the same as being.
So that's it? We broke the world, and the pieces don't— that's IT?
No. No no no, I did not climb all those stairs for "that's it"—
The Dawnsong called the old sun home. The Vespersong tried to make it stay.
Neither of them is ours.
We sing something new.
I cannot sing. I want that on record. I have been asked to stop by three separate choirs.
Sing anyway.

Wren starts. She doesn't know the song — nobody does; it hasn't been written yet. She sings the tide coming in at Lanternfall, and the smell of Nana Brisa's kitchen, and the sound her mother made when she laughed.
Ilse comes in under her, careful and exact — the hum she makes when she's stitching a wound.
Then Bram — terribly, loudly, completely off-key — and he does not stop.
Pip, with a gutter-song from Aurenne whose words are definitely not for children.
Corvin, an old Dawnguard marching tune, slowed down until it sounds like a lullaby.
And Sable, who has no song of her own — so she sings all of theirs back to them, a little wrong, and entirely hers.
The seven Shards melt together. Not into the old sun. Into something smaller, and stranger, and the color of no light any of them has ever seen.
It rises.
Evernoon is coming apart around them — gently, like frost in the morning. Marble turning to light. Bunting turning to birds.
Overhead there is a dawn. Not gold. A color nobody has a name for yet.
She walked toward it because she was scared of it. I never told anyone that. I never told anyone anything true about her. Only that she was gone.
And the Hierophant of Solmere, who has not raised his voice in forty years, puts his face in his hands and weeps like a boy of twelve.
Sable crosses the throne room and kneels beside him. After a moment, she takes his hand.
Sable. Wren gave it to me. Because of my hair.
Sable.
It suits you.
Will you— I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. Will you stay? Just until—
Yes.
Cassian. This is hers. It was always hers.
He opens it to the flyleaf. _For Lysa, who wants to know where the sun goes._
He is fading at the edges, the way the city is. He doesn't seem to mind. He is looking up at the new dawn the way a child looks at a kite.
Wren. What will you call it?
